title: IEEE PELS University Lab Kit
tools: CAD, 3D printing, client coordination, manufacturing and shipping
evidence: Printed bases · 200+ printed-part sets manufactured and shipped
imageAlt: White printed IEEE PELS lab-kit base with square nuts installed in slots in the mounting posts
description: Adapted lab-kit bases for printing without supports and managed manufacturing and shipping of more than 200 complete printed-part sets.
takeaway: I adapted the lab kit’s printed bases and managed manufacturing and shipping of more than 200 complete printed-part sets.
overviewHeading: From a mounting detail to a production run.
overview: The IEEE Power Electronics Society’s University Lab Kit gives students a platform for hands-on power-electronics experiments. At Illinois MakerLab, I adapted the supplied base designs for 3D printing and worked with the client on the mounting arrangement.

I designed fitted slots for square nuts so circuit boards could be screwed in, removed for debugging, and reinstalled without heat-set inserts or adhesive. I also adapted the bases to print without supports.
I then scaled production through MakerLab and managed manufacturing and shipping of more than 200 complete sets of printed parts. The electronics and other kit components were handled separately.

story.heading: A removable mount with fewer assembly steps
paragraphs: The boards needed a screw-fastened mounting arrangement. I used fitted square-nut slots in the printed posts so the connection could be taken apart and reassembled, without installing heat-set inserts or using adhesive.
Printing without supports also removed a support-cleanup step from the production workflow. The photographs show the current printed base with square nuts seated in its mounting posts.

story.heading: Following the parts through to delivery
paragraphs: My work extended beyond the CAD changes. I coordinated with the client on the mounting arrangement, scaled printing through MakerLab, and organized and managed manufacturing and shipping of the printed-part sets.

The outcome was more than 200 complete sets of printed components manufactured and shipped. This quantity refers to the printed parts; it does not include production of the electronics or the complete laboratory kit.

title: Tape Spring Hinge
tools: Abaqus, MATLAB, camera measurements, vibration and bending tests
imageAlt: Thin steel tape spring bent in a measurement fixture
takeaway: I tested a flexible steel hinge in several ways to find which parts of its behavior the model could predict.
overviewHeading: Checking a hinge against a real specimen.

description: Built and tested a flexible steel hinge, comparing its shape, vibration, and bending response with Abaqus models.
overview: A tape spring can fold and recover using the flexibility of a thin curved strip. I prepared a steel specimen and compared its shape, vibration, and bending response with models in Abaqus and MATLAB.
The second vibration frequency matched within about 5%, while other modes differed more. The nonlinear bending simulation also stopped before completing the measured response.

Checking several behaviors made the comparison more useful: a close result in one test could not establish that the model captured the hinge’s full motion. The project gave me measured evidence for where the assumptions needed further attention.

story.heading: Measuring the hinge before comparing it
paragraphs: I prepared the thin steel specimen and used camera measurements to record its shape. I combined those measurements with a tap test for vibration and a separate bending test, so each comparison addressed a different part of the hinge’s behavior.
The motion sequence shows the specimen changing shape. The vibration measurements came from a separate tap test.

story.heading: Where the predictions agreed
paragraphs: The second vibration mode measured 111.70 Hz, compared with a prediction of 117.20 Hz—a difference of about 5%. Other modes differed more. I analyzed the measurements in MATLAB alongside the Abaqus results rather than judging the model from its closest match alone.

story.heading: Where the comparison remained incomplete
paragraphs: The nonlinear bending simulation stopped before reproducing the full measured response. The plot shows that limit directly. Completing that response and investigating the test and modeling assumptions remained further work.

tools: NX CAD, rigid-panel geometry, 3D-printed panels, tape-hinge assembly

description: Designed and assembled printed folding mechanisms, adjusting panel thickness and clearance so solid parts could move together.
overview: A pattern that folds in paper can jam when its panels have thickness. I designed rigid-panel mechanisms in NX, changing panel thicknesses and adding cutouts to give the moving parts room.
I prepared the designs, assembled the printed panels with tape hinges, and checked their motion by hand. Nikhil submitted the print job on the Space Structures Lab-managed printer.

The Bennett-linkage prototype demonstrated coordinated folding, and a related Miura-Ori assembly explored another pattern. These were working demonstrations of the geometry; strength and repeated-use durability were not tested.

story.heading: Allowing for panel thickness
paragraphs: The paper models helped establish the folding motion. In NX, I translated that geometry into solid parts. I varied panel thickness and cut away material where needed so neighboring panels could pass one another as the mechanism folded.

story.heading: Assembling and checking the motion
paragraphs: I joined the printed panels with tape hinges and moved the Bennett-linkage prototype through its folding sequence. That physical check showed the coordinated movement of the assembled parts, beyond what the CAD views alone could show.

story.heading: Trying a second folding pattern
paragraphs: I also assembled a thick-panel Miura-Ori model and examined its motion. Together, the prototypes showed how thickness and clearance affect whether a folding pattern can work as a physical mechanism.

title: Thin Origami Bellows
tools: NX crease-pattern design, paper fabrication, tensile testing, data analysis
imageAlt: Paper bellows specimen and printed fixtures mounted in a tensile testing frame
takeaway: I designed and tested a paper bellows; the test showed why its attachments needed as much attention as its folds.
attribution: I performed CAD, fabrication, testing, and analysis. The report acknowledges fixture guidance from the Space Structures Lab.

description: Designed and folded a paper bellows, then tested how it opened under tension and examined tearing near its attachment.
overview: I designed a paper bellows to study how a folded structure opens under tension. I created the crease pattern in NX, made the specimen, and tested it using printed fixtures.
The single trial reached 48.1 N before tearing near an attachment. That result describes this specimen and test setup, rather than a repeatable strength rating.

The test made the load transfer into the paper a clear issue for further work. Better attachments and repeat tests would be needed to separate the bellows’ opening behavior from the limits of the setup.

story.heading: Making the bellows
paragraphs: I drew the crease pattern in NX, then scored and folded the paper into a bellows. Printed fixtures connected its ends to the tensile frame. I carried out the CAD, fabrication, testing, and analysis, with fixture guidance from the Space Structures Lab.

story.heading: Reading the force and the damage together
paragraphs: The trial recorded a peak of 48.1 N and tearing near an attachment. The record began with preload and covered limited movement, so it did not capture a complete opening cycle. I considered the measured force alongside where the paper tore, rather than treating the peak as an intrinsic property of the folding pattern.
The useful next step was to improve the attachments and repeat the test. Those changes were identified from the trial; they were not completed within this project.

title: Carbon-Epoxy I-Beam
tools: Composite layup, tooling, curing, load testing
imageAlt: Composite beam bagged and restrained in fabrication tooling
takeaway: I led the build of a composite beam and revised the manufacturing process when the first cure warped its flanges.
overviewHeading: Building a beam from the team’s design.
attribution: Team project. I led fabrication; numerical design and aggregate test results are credited to the team.

description: Led fabrication of a carbon-fiber beam, revising the core preparation and cure setup before the team’s load test.
overview: Our team designed a carbon-fiber I-beam for a 7,200 lbf load target. I led fabrication, turning the numerical design into a physical beam using the materials, tooling, and cure equipment available to us.

We changed the core preparation when foam filling proved impractical, then revised the cure setup after the flanges warped. The team’s tested Nomex-core beam reached 2,376 lbf—about one-third of the target.

The test exposed a substantial gap between the design prediction and the manufactured beam. My part of the project was working through the build decisions and documenting the process behind that result.

story.heading: Choosing a core we could manufacture
paragraphs: The initial plan used foam-filled Nomex honeycomb. Filling the core proved impractical, so we moved to unfilled Nomex bonded with adhesive film. I worked through the layup and assembly around the team’s design, available prepreg, and steel-channel tooling.

story.heading: Changing the cure setup
paragraphs: The initial cure left the flanges warped. We changed the beam’s orientation and added restraint during curing to address the distortion. This was a manufacturing problem we had to resolve before the beam could be tested.

story.heading: What the load test showed
paragraphs: The team measured a failure load of 2,376 lbf against the 7,200 lbf target. The build did not achieve the required load, and the result made the difference between an ideal numerical structure and the manufactured part clear. The report records the fabrication sequence and test for further investigation.

title: Bistable Composite Boom
tools: MATLAB, laminate modeling, composite fabrication, camera-based shape measurement

description: Modeled, built, and measured a carbon-fiber boom that holds both a coiled and an extended shape.
overview: A deployable boom needs to pack away compactly and hold a useful shape when extended. I modeled, fabricated, and measured a thin carbon-fiber specimen that could stay in either configuration without being held.
The measurements of how tightly each shape curved were within about 5% of the model’s predictions for this specimen. I then screened 5,476 simulated layer arrangements to explore alternatives.

That comparison showed a useful tradeoff: lowering the estimated energy needed to switch shapes also changed the coiled geometry. A design needed to meet both requirements. The alternative arrangements remained simulations.

story.heading: From laminate model to specimen
paragraphs: I used MATLAB to model a three-layer composite, then fabricated it on the available mold. Layer arrangement matters because it determines the shapes the thin structure can hold. Building a baseline gave me a real part to compare with the prediction.

story.heading: Measuring both shapes
paragraphs: I measured the extended and coiled configurations with stereo cameras. Their curvatures were within about 5% of the predicted values. I also adjusted model parameters to explore the remaining mismatch; fitting those same measurements was a calibration step, rather than a separate test of the model.

story.heading: Choosing what to optimize
paragraphs: I compared 5,476 modeled layer arrangements. Some lowered the estimated energy required to move between the two stable shapes, but they also changed the stored shape. The screen helped identify which candidates deserved closer study without treating the lowest energy as the only design objective.

description: Mapped how a proposed medical-drone control center would handle delivery requests, plan missions, and exchange information with aircraft and ground teams.
overview: A medical-drone delivery involves more than the aircraft. A request has to become a mission, the aircraft needs monitoring, and several groups need the right information. I developed a proposed command-and-control architecture around those responsibilities.

I created the operating concept, functional breakdown, requirements structure, and interface matrix. Keeping the focus on the control center made the scope manageable while showing its connections to aircraft, ground stations, customers, and external services.
The result was a documented systems design for review and further requirements development. It was not an operating delivery service or a flight-test project.

story.heading: Defining the control center’s responsibilities
paragraphs: I set the system boundary around the command-and-control center. That let me examine mission planning, aircraft monitoring, airspace coordination, and safety intervention while making the dependencies on other groups explicit.

story.heading: Tracing a request through the system
paragraphs: I broke the proposed operation into functions and mapped the information needed between them. The interface matrix recorded the exchanges across subsystem boundaries, giving the architecture a basis for review.
The output was a proposed architecture and a starting point for more detailed requirements. Numerical requirements still needed refinement before implementation and testing.

title: Functionally Graded Crash Boxes
tools: LS-DYNA, nonlinear impact modeling, comparative design analysis
imageAlt: Four simulated crash-box shapes during progressive collapse
takeaway: My thesis compared crash-box designs and showed how redistributing wall thickness changes their response to impact.
overviewHeading: Studying how a crash box absorbs impact.

report.title: Impact Analysis of Multi-Cell Crash Box Structures with Transverse Functionally Graded Thickness

figures.title: Progressive collapse in simulation
figures.caption: Four LS-DYNA states showing the modeled crash box folding during impact.
figures.alt: Four LS-DYNA simulation states showing a red crash box progressively crushing

figures.title: Uniform and graded wall thickness
figures.caption: The conventional multicell section (left) and a graded-thickness section (right). Both retain four cells while distributing wall material differently.
figures.alt: Side-by-side model cross sections showing a uniform four-cell tube and a four-cell tube with varying wall thickness.

description: Used impact simulations to study how internal walls and varying thickness change a crash box’s folding, energy absorption, and crushing force.
overview: A crash box absorbs energy by folding during an impact. In my undergraduate thesis, I studied how its internal walls and thickness distribution change that process.

I developed LS-DYNA models, checked the modeling approach against a published impact test, and compared designs under the same simulated conditions. One graded design absorbed 124% more energy per unit of crushed material than a plain tube, and 11.8% more than a conventional multicell tube.

The same design had a 15.8% lower mean crushing force than the multicell comparison. These simulation results showed a tradeoff to consider in design selection; the proposed structures were not physically tested.

story.heading: Comparing the wall layouts
paragraphs: I modeled plain, multicell, and graded-thickness tubes. Changing the wall thickness across a section let me study where the material influenced the folding sequence. Using common impact conditions made the numerical comparisons consistent.

story.heading: Checking the model and following the collapse
paragraphs: I used a physical impact test from published research as a benchmark for the modeling approach. That experiment was performed by the cited researchers; my work was the numerical modeling and design comparison.

I examined the progressive collapse alongside the energy and force results. The highlighted design improved energy absorption per crushed mass, but that measure uses the material crushed during the event, not the total component mass. Its lower mean crushing force also mattered to the comparison. Physical tests would be needed to assess the proposed designs further.
